title: High-titer convalescent serum from cats recovered from severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome protects SFTSV-infected mice.
abstract: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an emerging tick-borne zoonosis caused by severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) and is associated with high case-fatality rates in humans and cats. No vaccines or antiviral drugs are currently available for the prevention or treatment of feline SFTS. We hypothesized that some cats that recover from naturally acquired SFTS develop high neutralizing antibody titers and may serve as a source of convalescent serum for passive immunotherapy. We measured 80% plaque-reduction neutralization test (PRNT 80 ) titers in convalescent sera from six human SFTS survivors and 14 cats that had recovered from naturally acquired SFTS, and then evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of convalescent cat serum in SFTSV-infected, interferon receptor-deficient AG129 mice. Some SFTS-recovered cats exhibited high PRNT 80 titers. Passive administration of high-titer convalescent cat serum early after infection protected SFTSV-infected mice. A single dose given at 2 or 3 days post-infection completely protected mice, whereas treatment at 4 days post-infection resulted in 40% survival. In the repeated-dose experiment, early treatment was associated with lower blood viral RNA levels than controls at 6 dpi, and surviving mice also showed low viral RNA levels at 13 dpi. Sera from three additional SFTS-recovered cats also improved survival. Collectively, these findings indicate that some SFTS-recovered cats can develop high neutralizing antibody titers and that their sera can exert therapeutic effects in an SFTSV-infected mouse model, supporting further evaluation of passive immunotherapy as a treatment strategy for feline SFTS.

title: Demographic decomposition of changes in notifications of Japanese spotted fever, severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome, and scrub typhus in Japan, 2014-2016 versus 2022-2024
abstract: Notifications of several tick- and mite-borne infections in Japan have risen, and an increasing share of patients are aged 70 and over. Both the growth of the older population and change in age-specific notification rates can produce that pattern, while national and local population decline works in the opposite direction. This study decomposes the change in average annual notifications between 2014-2016 and 2022-2024 into three additive contributions - national population size, age composition across the published age classes, and age-class-specific notification rates - for Japanese spotted fever, severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome and scrub typhus, using the same population series, comparison periods and decomposition rule for all three. The decomposition averages over all permutations of the factors (Shapley-Shorrocks), so no separate interaction term remains and the result does not depend on substitution order. Contributions are reported in cases per year and per 100 baseline cases, alongside a fixed-rate standardised scenario, an eight-region four-factor decomposition, sex-specific analyses, scenario analyses for composition within the open 70-and-over class, a supplementary Poisson interval and a leave-one-year-out range. Only published aggregate statistics are used. The contributions are standardisation quantities, not causal effects, preventable case counts or infection counts, and the protocol fixes in advance how they may and may not be described. Scrub typhus is included as a disease with a different notification trend and is explicitly not a negative control. This registration is made before bulk retrieval of the source tables for all years; the information already viewed is enumerated rather than claiming that no data have been seen.

abstract: Abstract Background Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an acute infectious disease caused by severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV, also known as Dabie bandavirus), representing an emerging tick-borne disease. Complications such as encephalopathy and secondary invasive fungal infections significantly increase the mortality rate of this disease, for which no specific antiviral therapeutics are currently approved. Case Report: A 70-year-old male patient presented with persistent fever, thrombocytopenia and bleeding tendencies following a tick bite. His condition deteriorated rapidly, characterized by convulsions, cognitive impairment and multiple organ dysfunction, leading to a confirmed diagnosis of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome complicated by secondary invasive invasive aspergillosis. The patient’s life was successfully saved through a comprehensive clinical regimen, including early antiviral therapy with favipiravir, broad-spectrum anti-infective treatment, targeted antifungal therapy against Aspergillus with voriconazole, anti-inflammatory intervention with low-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, immune modulation using intravenous immunoglobulin, multiple sessions of therapeutic plasma exchange, liver protection, acid suppression, hemostasis and precise anticoagulation guided by dynamic risk assessments of hemorrhage and thrombosis. Following these multimodal interventions, the patient was smoothly weaned from mechanical ventilation and successfully extubated. His clinical indicators, viral load and inflammatory markers progressively declined alongside the recovery of organ function, ultimately resulting in a successful discharge. Conclusion This rare case of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome complicated by invasive aspergillosis highlights two key priorities in the management of critically ill older patients: close monitoring for neurological complications and secondary fungal infections, together with a multidimensional therapeutic approach incorporating antiviral therapy, plasma exchange for immunomodulation and targeted antifungal treatment.

title_zh: 老年患者新型布尼亚病毒感染合并侵袭性曲霉病的临床管理策略
source_body_en: Abstract Background Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an acute infectious disease caused by severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV, also known as Dabie bandavirus), representing an emerging tick-borne disease. Complications such as encephalopathy and secondary invasive fungal infections significantly increase the mortality rate of this disease, for which no specific antiviral therapeutics are currently approved. Case Report: A 70-year-old male patient presented with persistent fever, thrombocytopenia and bleeding tendencies following a tick bite. His condition deteriorated rapidly, characterized by convulsions, cognitive impairment and multiple organ dysfunction, leading to a confirmed diagnosis of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome complicated by secondary invasive invasive aspergillosis. The patient’s life was successfully saved through a comprehensive clinical regimen, including early antiviral therapy with favipiravir, broad-spectrum anti-infective treatment, targeted antifungal therapy against Aspergillus with voriconazole, anti-inflammatory intervention with low-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, immune modulation using intravenous immunoglobulin, multiple sessions of therapeutic plasma exchange, liver protection, acid suppression, hemostasis and precise anticoagulation guided by dynamic risk assessments of hemorrhage and thrombosis. Following these multimodal interventions, the patient was smoothly weaned from mechanical ventilation and successfully extubated. His clinical indicators, viral load and inflammatory markers progressively declined alongside the recovery of organ function, ultimately resulting in a successful discharge. Conclusion This rare case of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome complicated by invasive aspergillosis highlights two key priorities in the management of critically ill older patients: close monitoring for neurological complications and secondary fungal infections, together with a multidimensional therapeutic approach incorporating antiviral therapy, plasma exchange for immunomodulation and targeted antifungal treatment.
abstract_zh: 摘要 背景 发热伴血小板减少综合征(发热伴血小板减少综合征)是由发热伴血小板减少综合征病毒(SFTSV,也称为大别山布尼亚病毒)引起的急性传染病,代表一种新兴的人兽共患病。脑病和继发性侵袭性真菌感染等并发症显著增加了该病的死亡率,目前尚无针对该病的特异性治疗药物。病例:一名70岁男性患者因蜱咬后出现持续发热、血小板减少和出血倾向。其病情迅速恶化,表现为抽搐、认知功能障碍和多器官功能障碍,最终确诊为发热伴血小板减少综合征合并继发性侵袭性曲霉病。通过综合临床治疗方案,包括早期使用favipiravir进行抗病毒治疗、广谱抗感染治疗、针对曲霉菌的伏立康唑靶向抗真菌治疗、低剂量静脉甲基强的松龙抗炎干预、静脉免疫球蛋白免疫调节、多次治疗性血浆置换、保肝、抑酸、止血以及基于出血和血栓动态风险评估的精准抗凝治疗,患者生命得以成功挽救。经过这些多模式干预后,患者顺利脱离机械通气并成功拔管。其临床指标、病毒载量和炎症标志物随着器官功能的恢复而逐渐下降,最终实现成功出院。结论 这一罕见的发热伴血小板减少综合征合并侵袭性曲霉病病例突出了对重症老年患者管理的两个关键优先事项:密切监测神经系统并发症和继发性真菌感染,以及采用多维治疗策略,包括抗病毒治疗、血浆置换用于免疫调节和针对曲霉菌的靶向抗真菌治疗。

title: Inhibitory activity and mechanism of a scorpion-derived peptide BmKDfsin3 against SFTSV and HSV-1
abstract: UNLABELLED: Antiviral peptides, as an important source of antiviral drugs, will have significant application value and potential in the field of viral prevention and treatment. Therefore, it is of great significance to discover broad-spectrum, highly efficient, and low-toxicity antiviral peptides. Here, we found that the scorpion venom peptide BmKDfsin3 not only concentration-dependently inhibited the replication of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) but also suppressed the replication of herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) in A549 cells. The results of antiviral phase assays showed that BmKDfsin3 mainly inhibited the post-entry stage of the life cycle of these two viruses. Mechanistically, BmKDfsin3 effectively suppressed the activation of p38 induced by SFTSV and HSV-1 infections. Furthermore, using poly(I:C) as a viral mimic, we found that BmKDfsin3 enhanced type I and III interferon signaling pathways by activating the transcription factors p52 and IRF3. Importantly, BmKDfsin3 exhibited good biosafety, including low cytotoxicity, hemolytic activity, and mouse toxicity. Overall, BmKDfsin3 was revealed to be a natural bioactive peptide with good biological safety, potent antiviral activity, and a broad antiviral spectrum. IMPORTANCE: The scorpion venom peptide BmKDfsin3 mediates antiviral activity through a dual mechanism: it limits viral replication by inhibiting the exploitation of host p38 signaling by SFTSV and HSV-1, and it promotes host immune responses by activating transcription factors p52 and IRF3 to enhance type I and III interferon (IFN) signaling. This synergy between "inhibiting virus-dependent pathway" and "activating host immunity" confers potent, broad-spectrum antiviral activity upon BmKDfsin3, resulting in significant dose-dependent inhibition against phylogenetically distinct RNA (SFTSV) and DNA (HSV-1) viruses. Importantly, the peptide exhibits minimal cytotoxicity, hemolytic activity, and in vivo toxicity. This study provides new insights into how a single-peptide molecule achieves efficient, broad-spectrum antiviral activity by concurrently targeting virus-dependent and host immune pathways, highlighting the therapeutic potential of antiviral peptides in broad-spectrum drug design.

title: Epidemiology and spillover risk of SFTSV in animals across East Asia
abstract: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an emerging tick‐borne zoonosis in East Asia, yet the contribution of animals to virus maintenance and spillover remains incompletely characterized. This review synthesizes current evidence of SFTS virus (SFTSV) infection across domestic livestock, companion animals, wildlife, and captive species, focusing on host range, geographic distribution, diagnostics, and reports of viral RNA and virus isolation. Available data indicate that SFTSV exposure and infection occur across a broad range of animal hosts, supporting a multi-host ecological framework rather than a simple single-reservoir interpretation. Domestic ruminants frequently exhibit high seroprevalence and may function as sentinels of enzootic activity, while occasional virus isolation from cattle demonstrates that viable virus can be recovered from naturally infected livestock, although this does not establish reservoir or amplification competence. Companion animals are considered a potential interface for interspecies transmission, as some studies have documented severe clinical disease, high viral loads, and cat-associated human transmission events supported by varying levels of epidemiological and genomic evidence. Studies in wildlife further document exposure and natural infection across diverse taxa, although their specific roles in viral maintenance remain unresolved. Interpretation of these findings depends heavily on the diagnostic modality: serology primarily indicates prior exposure, RNA detection supports current or recent infection, and virus isolation demonstrates that viable virus was present in the sampled material. Integrating animal infection data within an ecological framework reveals major knowledge gaps related to reservoir competence, infectious shedding, phylogenetic connections among animal, tick, and human cases, and implications for prevention. The review underscores the need for One Health surveillance that incorporates clinical data from companion animals and applies evidence‐based interpretation to improve recognition of animal–human interfaces associated with potential spillover risk.

Available data indicate that SFTSV exposure and infection occur across a broad range of animal hosts, supporting a multi-host ecological framework rather than a simple single-reservoir interpretation. Domestic ruminants frequently exhibit high seroprevalence and may function as sentinels of enzootic activity, while occasional virus isolation from cattle demonstrates that viable virus can be recovered from naturally infected livestock, although this does not establish reservoir or amplification competence. Companion animals are considered a potential interface for interspecies transmission, as some studies have documented severe clinical disease, high viral loads, and cat-associated human transmission events supported by varying levels of epidemiological and genomic evidence. Studies in wildlife further document exposure and natural infection across diverse taxa, although their specific roles in viral maintenance remain unresolved. Interpretation of these findings depends heavily on the diagnostic modality: serology primarily indicates prior exposure, RNA detection supports current or recent infection, and virus isolation demonstrates that viable virus was present in the sampled material. Integrating animal infection data within an ecological framework reveals major knowledge gaps related to reservoir competence, infectious shedding, phylogenetic connections among animal, tick, and human cases, and implications for prevention. The review underscores the need for One Health surveillance that incorporates clinical data from companion animals and applies evidence‐based interpretation to improve recognition of animal–human interfaces associated with potential spillover risk.

full_text: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), caused by Dabie bandavirus, is associated with high mortality among intensive care unit (ICU) patients; however, the integrated proteomic–metabolomic mechanisms underlying fatal outcomes remain poorly characterized. This prospective cohort study enrolled 68 patients with SFTS, who were admitted to the ICU and classified them as survivors (n = 33) or non-survivors (n = 35) according to their 28-day clinical outcomes. Untargeted metabolomic profiling using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry and quantitative proteomic profiling using data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry were performed on plasma samples collected at ICU admission. Multivariable analysis, pathway enrichment analysis, correlation analysis, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis were used to identify potential prognostic biomarkers and characterize molecular associations. Non-survivors exhibited more severe multi-organ injury and systemic inflammation. Metabolomic profiling revealed marked disruption of tryptophan metabolism: L-tryptophan levels were decreased, whereas kynurenine and its downstream metabolites (kynurenic acid [KA], 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid [3-HAA], xanthurenic acid [XA], and 5-hydroxyindolepyruvate [5-HIP]) were increased, suggesting activation of the kynurenine pathway. The four core tryptophan metabolites yielded a combined area under the curve (AUC) of 0.934 for predicting 28-day mortality and were correlated with indicators of renal function and coagulation. Proteomic profiling identified 200 differentially expressed proteins: proteins upregulated in survivors were enriched in the proteasome pathway, whereas those upregulated in non-survivors were enriched in the IL-17 pathway and other inflammatory and immune pathways. Integrated analysis revealed that the four tryptophan metabolites were associated with 20 differentially expressed proteins, six of which showed robust associations within outcome subgroups. Collectively, tryptophan metabolic disturbances coupled with inflammatory proteomic features may characterize fatal severe SFTS, and the identified metabolite–protein signatures may serve as promising prognostic biomarkers and potential therapeutic targets in critically ill patients. 2Materials and methods2.1Study design and participantsThis prospective cohort study included patients with severe SFTS who were admitted to the ICU between July 2019 and October 2023. According to their 28-day clinical outcomes, patients were divided into survivor (n = 33) and non-survivor (n = 35) groups. All specimens were collected in the Department of Critical Care Medicine, Yantai Qishan Hospital. The study was approved by the Ethics Review Committee of Yantai Qishan Hospital (approval no. 202503). The participants were informed about the research and its potential risks and provided written informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The inclusion criteria (11) were as follows: (1) detection of novel bunyavirus nucleic acids in blood samples, confirmed by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) in the laboratory, and (2) fulfillment of the criteria for severe and critical disease classification outlined in the Consensus on Diagnosis and Treatment of Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (2022 Edition). The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) clinically suspected severe SFTS with an alternative diagnosis established subsequently; (2) incomplete clinical data; (3) age <16 years; (4) immunocompromised status, defined as glucocorticoid or immunosuppressant use within 1 month, human immunodeficiency virus infection, solid or hematological malignancy, long-term nursing home residency, or hospitalization within 90 days; and (5) co-infection with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, hepatitis C virus, Brucella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, or Treponema pallidum to avoid potential confounding.2.2Clinical data and plasma sample collectionBaseline demographic and clinical data were obtained from electronic medical records, including age, sex, comorbidities, heart rate, maximum body temperature, respiratory rate, and the interval between disease onset and ICU admission. The lowest Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score within 24 h before ICU admission and before sedation was recorded, along with altered mental status, bleeding events, and secondary infections. The primary endpoint was 28-day mortality after ICU admission. Laboratory parameters measured within 24 h of ICU admission included viral load, lactate, and other relevant laboratory indicators. Peripheral venous blood samples were collected in the morning within 24 h after ICU admission. All enrolled patients were fasting at the time of sampling. Blood was collected in anticoagulant tubes and immediately transported to the laboratory, where the samples were centrifuged at 1, 500 × g for 15 min. The upper plasma layer was collected and stored at −80 °C until further analysis. Before analysis, plasma samples were thawed on ice at 4 °C. To ensure sample quality, all samples included in this study underwent only one freeze–thaw cycle. To minimize potential bias, the sample-processing and LC-MS/MS injection orders were randomized between the survivor and non-survivor groups.2.3Metabolite extraction and LC-MS/MS analysisAll plasma samples were thawed on ice and vortexed vigorously. Hydrophilic metabolites were extracted using pre-cooled methanol. Briefly, 100 μL of homogenized plasma was mixed with 300 μL of pre-cooled methanol, vortexed thoroughly, and incubated at −20 °C for 30 min. The supernatants were then collected for instrumental analysis. Chromatographic separation was performed using a SHIMADZU-LC30 ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography system equipped with an ACQUITY UPLC® HSS T3 column (2.1×100 mm, 1.8 μm) (Waters, Milford, MA, USA) and mass spectrometric analysis was performed using a QE Plus mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with electrospray ionization in both positive and negative modes (Supplementary Information File S1). Raw mass spectrometry data were processed using MSDIAL software for peak alignment, retention-time correction, and peak-area extraction. Metabolite structures were identified by accurate-mass matching (mass tolerance <20 ppm) and MS2 spectrum matching (mass tolerance <0.01 Da) against public databases, including the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB), and a self-established in-house database. Ion peaks with >50% missing values within either group were excluded from subsequent statistical analyses. Before statistical analysis, all data were normalized to the total peak area to improve comparability and reduce variation.To monitor analytical stability, quality control (QC) samples prepared by pooling equal volumes of all plasma samples were injected after every 15 experimental samples. QC assessment included comparison of base peak chromatograms of QC samples in both positive and negative ion modes, with consistent peak intensities and retention times across injections indicating minimal instrument variation, as well as principal component analysis of QC samples, which showed tight clustering and satisfactory repeatability. Because all samples were analyzed in a single batch and QC evaluation indicated stable instrument performance, no inter-batch correction was required.2.4Proteome sample preparation and data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry data analysisSamples were thawed at 4 °C, and 2 μL of each sample was dissolved in 48 μL of UA buffer, incubated at 37 °C for 1 h, sonicated for 2 min, centrifuged, and then incubated at 4 °C for 20 min. The supernatants were collected. Low-abundance proteins were enriched using a low-abundance protein enrichment kit. An appropriate volume of 1 M DTT was added to the enriched samples to achieve a final concentration of 100 mM, followed by incubation at 37 °C for 30 min and cooling to 24 °C. Subsequently, an appropriate volume of IAA was added to achieve a final concentration of 50 mM, and the samples were incubated at room temperature for 30 min in the dark. Each sample was diluted sixfold with 50 mM NH4HCO3, after which 8 μg of Trypsin was added, and the resulting mixture was vortexed at 600 rpm for 1 min and incubated at 37 °C for 20 h. The enzymatically digested samples were acidified with an appropriate volume of TFA, and the peptides were desalted using a C18 cartridge and reconstituted in 0.1% FA; peptide concentrations were then determined before LC-MS analysis. Appropriate amounts of peptides from each sample were separated using a Vanquish Neo UHPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) (Supplementary Information File S2).After peptide separation, DIA mass spectrometry was performed using an Orbitrap Astral mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The total analysis duration was 8 min, with an electrospray voltage of 2.2 kV in positive-ion detection mode. The precursor-ion scan range was 380–980 m/z, the full scan resolution was 240, 000, the AGC target was 500%, and the maximum ion injection time (IT) for the full scan was 3 ms. The MS2 parameters were as follows: resolution, 80, 000; AGC target, 500%; maximum IT, 3 ms; RF lens, 40%; activation type, HCD; isolation window, 2 Th; normalized collision energy, 25%; and cycle time, 0.6 s.All mass spectrometry data were processed using DIA-NN software for database searching and quantitative analysis of the DIA mass spectrometry data. The database used was the Swiss-Prot-Homo sapiens (Human) [9606]-reviewed-20421-20250908-iRT.fasta database. Subsequently, statistical analyses were performed on the qualitative and quantitative DIA proteomic results. Each sample was prepared independently and, after enzymatic protein digestion, subjected to DIA analysis. The resulting raw DIA mass spectrometry files were imported into DIA-NN for analysis using a q value threshold of ≤0.01.2.5Omics data processing, bioinformatics, and statistical analysisProteins and metabolites with valid measurements in fewer than 50% of samples in either group were excluded from further analyses. For metabolomics, differential metabolites were identified using the OPLS-DA model with variable importance in projection (VIP) >1.0, combined with univariate analysis (P < 0.05), an approach suited to the high-dimensional and multicollinear nature of metabolomic data. Metabolites were compared between survivors and non-survivors. Based on the intensity ratio of survivors/non-survivors, up-regulated metabolites denote higher abundance in non-survivors, while down-regulated metabolites denote higher abundance in survivors. For proteomics, differentially expressed proteins were defined based on a fold-change threshold (|FC| ≥ 1.5) and P < 0.05. The FC-based criterion was adopted because proteomic datasets typically contain fewer and more directly interpretable features than metabolomic datasets, for which multivariable filtering (e.g., VIP) is more commonly applied.Correlation analysis was used to evaluate associations between the four tryptophan metabolites and plasma proteins, as well as between the metabolites and clinical parameters. To determine whether these associations were independent of intergroup differences, correlations were calculated separately in the overall cohort (n = 68) and in the survivor (n = 33) and non-survivor (n = 35) groups. Within each stratum, P values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg method to control the FDR. In the overall cohort, proteins with |r| ≥0.35 and P < 0.05 were considered significantly correlated with the corresponding metabolite and were eligible for inclusion in the integrated metabolite–protein network. Associations that remained significant (P < 0.05) within either subgroup were defined as robust associations.Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were constructed to assess the discriminative value of differential metabolites and proteins for 28-day mortality in patients with severe SFTS. The area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, and 95% confidence interval (95% CI) were calculated. Categorical variables are presented as frequencies and percentages, whereas continuous variables are expressed as medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs). Continuous variables were compared between groups using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test or Kruskal–Wallis test, whereas categorical variables were analyzed using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test. Multiple-testing correction was performed using the Benjamini–Hochberg method. All statistical tests were two-tailed, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were performed using R, SPSS version 19.0, MedCalc version 15.8, and MetaboAnalyst version 4.0 (Wishart Research Group, University of Alberta, Canada). full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionSevere fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) poses a serious public health threat in East Asia, with substantially higher mortality among critically ill patients than in the general SFTS population. Clinical outcomes in severe SFTS are highly heterogeneous (1–4), reflecting complex host–virus interactions, dysregulated systemic inflammation, and progressive multi-organ dysfunction. In this context, integrated proteomic and metabolomic approaches have emerged as powerful tools for characterizing molecular changes associated with disease progression, identifying potential prognostic biomarkers, and informing the investigation of therapeutic targets in severe viral infections. Accumulating evidence supports the utility of omics strategies for investigating SFTS pathogenesis. Zhao et al. (5) demonstrated that proteomic profiling identifies dysregulated proteins involved in multiple cellular and immune processes in SFTS patients and established a proteasome-centered regulatory axis associated with adverse outcomes. Park et al. (6), by combining targeted proteomics with single-cell transcriptomics, characterized the peripheral blood immune landscape in SFTS and showed that, in fatal cases, SFTSV infection was associated with excessive inflammatory cascades involving proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines, accompanied by aberrant suppression of adaptive immunity. Zhu et al. (7) reported that serum metabolomic profiling of acute-phase SFTS patients linked perturbations in multiple metabolic pathways, particularly sphingolipid metabolism, to poor prognosis. Despite the considerable potential of multi-omics integration in severe viral infections (8–10), few studies have focused specifically on critically ill SFTS patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU), and the interplay between metabolic disturbances and proteomic dysregulation in fatal outcomes remains poorly characterized. This study provides the first integrated proteomic–metabolomic analysis of ICU patients with severe SFTS stratified by 28-day outcomes, aiming to characterize the metabolic and proteomic features associated with fatal disease.Consistent with previous clinical observations (11), baseline characteristics indicated a more severe disease phenotype in non-survivors, including lower Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores, higher SFTSV RNA loads, more pronounced systemic inflammation, multi-organ dysfunction involving the liver, kidney, and myocardium, coagulation disturbances, and reduced CD4+ and CD8+ T-lymphocyte counts. These findings further support the association of dysregulated host immune responses, systemic inflammation, and multi-organ injury with death in severe SFTS.The central finding of this study is the marked divergence in metabolite and protein profiles and signaling pathways between survivors and fatal cases. Among the perturbed pathways, tryptophan metabolism showed the strongest enrichment (hsa00380; 10/106 metabolites; adjusted P = 0.001), consistent with previous urine metabolomic findings identifying tryptophan metabolism as a major perturbed pathway in SFTS (12). As an essential amino acid, tryptophan participates in diverse physiological processes, including neuronal function, immune regulation, and intestinal homeostasis (13). In mammals, free tryptophan is predominantly catabolized via the kynurenine pathway, which is initiated by the rate-limiting enzymes IDO1 and TDO (14, 15). Our data showed significantly lower L-tryptophan (P = 0.0067) and higher levels of kynurenine and its downstream products KA, 3-HAA, XA, and 5-HIP in non-survivors (Supplementary Information Table S2). This pattern of lower substrate levels and higher product levels yields a metabolite signature consistent with enhanced kynurenine pathway activity in the setting of infection and critical illness (16–18). In COVID-19 and sepsis, elevated kynurenine-to-tryptophan ratios have been associated with disease severity and mortality (16, 18). Notably, a urine metabolomic study of SFTS likewise identified tryptophan metabolism as the top pathway distinguishing fatal from surviving patients, with elevated 5-HIAA, kynurenine, 5-HTP, and 3-HAA in fatal cases (12), supporting our findings in an independent biospecimen dimension. Importantly, our plasma-based observations suggest, but do not establish, activation of the kynurenine pathway; enzyme activities and metabolic fluxes were not directly measured, a limitation addressed below. Kynurenine pathway metabolites exert broad immunomodulatory effects: kynurenine is an endogenous ligand of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) (19); 3-HAA modulates T-cell function and may promote an imbalance between Th17 and regulatory T cells (20, 21); and KA has been positively correlated with inflammatory cytokines and chemokines and negatively correlated with T-cell responses in severe viral infections such as COVID-19 (22). These metabolite-mediated immunomodulatory actions may contribute to immune dysregulation in fatal SFTS. Moreover, the positive correlation of 3-HAA with renal function indicators (BUN and Cys-C) suggests that impaired renal clearance may contribute to metabolite accumulation in fatal cases, a phenomenon also reported in COVID-19, where kynurenine metabolites correlate with renal status and IL-6 levels (17). Altered tryptophan metabolism may thus reflect enhanced IDO/TDO activity together with hepatic and renal dysfunction and the hyperinflammatory, hypercatabolic state of critical illness; these potential mechanisms warrant further investigation.Beyond tryptophan metabolism, purine catabolism was also associated with fatal SFTS: xanthine and uric acid were significantly higher in non-survivors (Supplementary Information Table S2), consistent with the enrichment of nucleotide metabolism. Purine catabolism can generate reactive oxygen species, and uric acid can act as a damage-associated molecular pattern to promote inflammation (23, 24). Accordingly, serum adenosine deaminase (ADA), a key enzyme in purine catabolism that catalyzes the deamination of adenosine to inosine (25), was elevated in fatal SFTS patients and correlated with IL-6, TNF-α, and multi-organ failure (26). Enhanced purine turnover has likewise been observed in COVID-19 non-survivors (27). Together with the elevated purine catabolites in non-survivors, these data support increased purine catabolism in fatal SFTS, although causal roles require functional validation.Complementing the metabolomic findings, proteomic analysis identified 200 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) between the two groups. (5). In contrast, proteins upregulated in non-survivors were mainly associated with IL-17 signaling, TNF/NF-κB signaling, chemokine signaling, and cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction pathways, which are involved in inflammation and immune regulation, suggesting more intense inflammatory responses in fatal cases. Notably, four key proteins (SHROOM3, SEPSECS, MYH11, and PIGW) have been reported to have prognostic value (28, 29). These divergent expression profiles suggest that protein homeostasis may be relatively preserved in survivors, whereas fatal cases are characterized by greater activation of inflammatory signaling pathways. title_original: Integrated proteomic and metabolomic profiling characterizes tryptophan metabolic disturbance associated with mortality in ICU-admitted SFTS patients

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to characterize the integrated proteomic and metabolomic mechanisms underlying mortality in ICU-admitted SFTS patients, as SFTS remains a poorly understood public health threat with high mortality rates in severe cases.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A prospective cohort study was conducted on ICU-admitted patients with severe SFTS between July 2019 and October 2023, dividing them into survivor (n = 33) and non-survivor (n = 35) groups based on 28-day clinical outcomes.
analysis.methods: Baseline demographic and clinical data were collected from electronic medical records, and laboratory parameters such as viral load, lactate, and other indicators were measured within 24 h of ICU admission. Specimens were collected in the Department of Critical Care Medicine, Yantai Qishan Hospital, and the study was approved by the Ethics Review Committee of Yantai Qishan Hospital.
analysis.main_results: No statistically significant differences were observed in demographic characteristics or most comorbidities between the survivor and non-survivor groups (all P > 0.05). However, the non-survivor group had significantly lower median GCS (9.0 vs. 11.0, P = 0.002), higher median viral RNA copy number (1,150,000 vs. 1,000,000, P < 0.05), and elevated levels of lactate, PCT, IL-6, and ferritin (all P < 0.05). analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study identified marked disruption of tryptophan metabolism in non-survivors, with decreased L-tryptophan and increased kynurenine pathway metabolites, suggesting a potential link between metabolic disturbances and adverse outcomes in SFTS.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings may inform the development of targeted diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for SFTS, particularly in identifying metabolic biomarkers associated with mortality in critically ill patients.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study had a limited sample size and potential confounding factors, such as co-infections and immunocompromised status, which were excluded. The evidence is moderate due to these limitations and the focus on observational data.

The study collected clinical data and laboratory parameters, including GCS scores, viral load, and inflammatory markers. Results showed no significant differences in demographics or comorbidities but highlighted more severe clinical and laboratory features in non-survivors. Metabolomic profiling revealed significant tryptophan metabolic disturbances, with decreased L-tryptophan and increased kynurenine pathway metabolites in non-survivors. These findings suggest a potential role for metabolic biomarkers in predicting mortality in SFTS. The study's limitations include a small sample size and exclusion of certain confounding factors, resulting in moderate evidence strength.
